To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we give new group testing algorithms, that we prove to be more efficient than previous ones, that are concisely parallelizable, and that we show how they can be used to efficiently solve dead sensor diagnosis in wireless ad hoc networks and MAC resolution.

(a) we have developed new adaptive group-testing algorithms that can be used to solve two problems that have not been addressed before; (b) we have shown that these algorithms can be implemented on a parallel architecture; (c) we have shown the algorithms to be provably more efficient, and we have given a lower bound that proves that they are optimal for certain response models.

(1) we give new adaptive group testing algorithms that are more efficient for certain generalized response models, (2) we give parallel algorithms for dead-sensor diagnosis, and (3) our algorithms can be applied to MAC resolution as well.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a new approach for solving generalized group testing problems, which has led to more efficient algorithms than previous approaches for solving dead sensor diagnosis and MAC resolution problems.
we give efficient algorithms for dead sensor identification and conflict resolution on MAC, and prove that they are the best possible.
we give the first parallel algorithms for dead sensors diagnosis and multiple access conflict resolution, which are more efficient than the previous sequential algorithms.
The main takeaway from our work is that

non-binary group-testing models are useful for solving a wide variety of problems in distributed systems, and that the parallelism inherent in our algorithms makes them particularly suitable for implementation in wireless networks.
the use of non-binary tests can significantly reduce the number of tests needed to solve group testing problems, and this can be exploited in the context of MACs.
we show how to efficiently identify dead sensors in a wireless network and resolve broadcast conflicts on a MAC using group testing algorithms, which can be implemented in a distributed fashion.
